15060:
When squat is used as an adjective, it describes something — or someone — that is noticeably short in height but wide or thick in body. Think of it as something that looks "pushed down" or "compressed." The height is less than you would naturally expect, given how wide or broad the thing is.

The word is all about proportion. Something squat doesn't just mean short, and it doesn't just mean wide. It means both at once — so short that the width stands out, creating a chunky, stubby, or dumpy overall shape.

Imagine a normal glass and a normal can of soda side by side. Now imagine someone pressed their hand on top of that glass and squashed it downward — suddenly it's shorter, the same width, and looks almost "squished." That is the visual feeling of "squat."

So the word captures:

  • Low height (shorter than typical or expected)
  • Noticeable width or thickness relative to that height
  • The overall impression of something that looks compressed, chunky, or stumpy

This adjective is very flexible. It can describe:

People:
A squat person is someone who is short and broadly built — stocky, thick-limbed, and solid-looking. It is not about being overweight specifically; it's about the overall short-and-wide shape of the body.

"A squat, muscular man stood at the entrance of the warehouse."

Buildings and structures:
A squat building is one that sits low to the ground and appears wide relative to its height — the opposite of a tall, slender tower.

"The squat stone church had stood in that village for three centuries."
"A row of squat concrete bunkers lined the coastline."

Objects:
Any object that is noticeably short and wide for its type can be called squat.

"She poured the oil from a squat, dark-green bottle."
"The squat little lamp barely lit the corner of the room."

Plants and trees:

"A squat cactus sat on the windowsill, barely taller than a coffee mug."
The Feel and Connotation of the Word

"Squat" as an adjective is almost always neutral to mildly negative in tone. It is not a word of admiration. When you call a building squat, you are suggesting it lacks elegance or height. When you call a person squat, you are describing their build in a blunt, unflattering way — it's not considered a compliment. Writers use it to create an image of something unimpressive, heavy, ungainly, or plain.

That said, it is not a harsh insult either. It is more like a matter-of-fact physical description, delivered with a slightly critical or unenthusiastic eye.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "A tall, graceful tower rose above the city."
  • "A squat, ugly tower huddled between the buildings."

You can feel the difference in attitude. "Squat" drags the image downward — literally and emotionally.
How It Differs from Similar Words

• Short simply means low in height. A squat thing is short and wide. A tall, thin person can never be called squat, but a short, thin person would not typically be called squat either — the width or thickness matters.
  • Fat refers to excess body weight or flesh. A squat person may or may not be fat — the word focuses on the shape and proportions of the body, not on body fat.
  • Stocky is the closest near-synonym for people and means short and strongly built. "Stocky" is more neutral and even slightly positive (suggesting sturdiness), while "squat" leans more unflattering.
  • Stubby is similar but is used more for small individual body parts or small objects (stubby fingers, a stubby pencil), rather than whole people or buildings.
  • Dumpy is close in meaning but sounds even more negative and is almost exclusively used for people.
Depending on the context, squat can be replaced by: stocky, thickset, chunky, stumpy, stubby, low-slung, dumpy, heavyset.
The opposites of squat include: tall, slender, willowy, lanky, towering, statuesque.

If you remember just one thing: squat = short + wide, in a way that looks compressed or squashed. It applies to people, buildings, and objects. Its tone is neutral-to-unflattering, and it always draws attention to the disproportionate relationship between low height and notable width or thickness.
15061: "Squat" has two distinct meanings as a verb. Both are common and important to know.
Meaning 1: A physical position (the most common meaning)

To squat means to lower your body by bending your knees deeply, so that your bottom moves close to the ground — but does not touch it — while your feet stay flat on the floor.

Think of it like this: imagine a frog sitting still. Its legs are bent, its body is low, and its feet are on the ground. That is a squat position. Or think of a child crouching down to look at an insect on the ground. That, too, is squatting.

The key features of a squat are:

  • Your knees are deeply bent.
  • Your feet are flat on the ground (not raised on your toes).
  • Your bottom is hanging low, close to the floor, but not resting on anything.
  • Your body is balanced on your bent legs.

Example sentences:

  • She squatted down to pick up the coin from the floor.
  • He squatted beside the child to speak to her at eye level.
  • The mechanic squatted under the car to check the engine.

How "squat" differs from similar-looking words

Since learners often confuse squat with crouch, kneel, and sit, here is a clear breakdown:

Squat vs. Crouch:
These two are very close in meaning, and people often use them interchangeably. However, there is a subtle difference. When you crouch, you are often on the balls of your feet (your heels may be slightly off the ground), and the position feels more tense and alert — like you're ready to spring up or move quickly. When you squat, your feet are fully flat on the ground, and the position feels more settled and stable. A squat is generally lower and deeper than a crouch.

Squat vs. Kneel:
When you kneel, one or both of your knees actually touch the ground. When you squat, your knees are bent but they are in the air — they do not touch the ground. Your body weight is held up by your leg muscles in a squat.

Squat vs. Sit:
When you sit, your bottom rests on something — a chair, the floor, a surface. When you squat, your bottom is hovering above the ground. Nothing supports your weight except your legs.

Squatting as exercise

In fitness and sports, "to squat" refers to the specific exercise where you repeatedly move your body down into the squat position and back up again, usually to build strength in your legs, thighs, and hips. People do this with their own body weight or with a weighted bar resting on their shoulders.

Example:

  • He squatted 100 kilograms at the gym today.
  • The coach told the team to squat 20 times.
Meaning 2: To occupy a place illegally (without permission or payment)

To squat also means to move into and live in a building or on a piece of land that does not belong to you, without the owner's permission, and without paying any rent or fee.

This typically happens when a building is empty or abandoned, and someone who needs shelter moves in and lives there without any legal right to do so. The act is generally illegal in most places, though the laws vary by country. A person who does this is called a squatter.

Example sentences:

  • After losing their home, the family squatted in an abandoned warehouse.
  • The protesters squatted on the empty land for several weeks.
  • Dozens of squatters were found to be squatting in the derelict building.
A useful way to remember both meanings

Both meanings share one underlying idea: occupying a space without full, formal, proper support.

In the physical sense, you are occupying a low position without proper support (no chair, no floor beneath your bottom — just your own muscles holding you up).

In the legal sense, you are occupying a space without proper support (no lease, no permission, no ownership).

UseWhat it means
PhysicalTo bend your knees deeply and lower your body close to the ground, feet flat, bottom in the air
LegalTo live in or occupy a property that isn't yours, without permission or payment

(The physical meaning is far more common in everyday language.)
15062:
A squatter is a person who moves into and lives in a place — usually a building or a piece of land — that does not belong to them, without the owner's permission, without paying rent, and without any legal right to be there.

Think of it this way: imagine a house that has been empty and abandoned for years. Nobody lives in it, nobody is watching it. One day, a person simply walks in, sets up their belongings, and starts living there as if it were their home. That person is a squatter. They didn't buy the property. They didn't sign a lease. They didn't ask anyone. They just occupied it.

The verb behind this word is "to squat," which in this context means to settle on or occupy a place without any legal claim to it.

People become squatters for a variety of reasons, most often connected to hardship:

  • Poverty and homelessness — They cannot afford to rent or buy a place to live, so they occupy an empty building just to have shelter.
  • Lack of housing — In many cities, especially in developing countries, there is simply not enough affordable housing for everyone, so large groups of people settle on unused land and build makeshift homes.
  • Political protest — Some squatters deliberately occupy unused properties as a form of social or political protest, arguing that it is wrong for buildings to sit empty while people are homeless.
  • Seeking land — Historically, people moved onto unoccupied land (often government-owned) to farm it and build a life, hoping to claim it as their own over time.
Two Main Contexts: Modern and Historical

1. The Modern Meaning (Most Common)

Today, when people say "squatter," they almost always mean someone who is occupying an empty or abandoned property without permission. This is the universal, everyday meaning.

This could be:

  • A homeless person who moves into an abandoned house in a city.
  • A group of activists who occupy an empty commercial building to protest housing shortages.
  • A family in a developing country who builds a shack on unused land at the edge of a city because they have nowhere else to go.

2. The Historical Meaning (Australia and the American West)

The word "squatter" also has important historical meanings that are quite different in tone — and even somewhat positive.

In Australian history, squatters were wealthy pastoralists (farmers who raised sheep and cattle) who moved their livestock onto vast stretches of government-owned land in the 18th and 19th centuries without any formal permission or license to do so. Over time, many of these squatters became extremely powerful and influential — they formed the backbone of Australia's rural elite. Eventually, many of them were granted formal legal rights to the land they occupied. So in Australian history, calling someone a "squatter" carries a sense of being a pioneering, if unauthorised, landowner — not a homeless person. This historical class of people is still known as "the squattocracy" (a word combining squatter and aristocracy).

In American history, squatters were settlers who moved onto unsettled or government-owned land on the frontier, particularly in the 18th and 19th centuries, without any legal title. They would clear the land, build homes, and farm it — gambling that they would eventually be allowed to purchase it legally. Many of America's early settlements grew from squatting.

This is one of the most fascinating and important concepts connected to the word "squatter," and it is very real in law.

In many countries, if a squatter occupies a piece of land or property openly, continuously, and without the owner's objection for a long enough period of time (which varies by country and region — it could be anywhere from 5 to 20+ years), they may actually earn the legal right to own that property. This legal principle is called adverse possession, but it is commonly known as squatter's rights.

The idea behind it is practical: if a property owner completely ignores their property and never challenges someone living on it for many years, the law in many places recognises the person who has actually been using and maintaining the land as its rightful owner. The law essentially asks, "Who has been acting like the real owner all along?"

This does not happen easily or automatically. The squatter usually has to meet very strict legal conditions, and the process is complex. But it is a genuine legal concept, not a myth.

In many parts of the world — particularly in rapidly growing cities in Africa, Asia, and Latin America — large communities of squatters form together in what are called squatter settlements. These are areas, usually on the edges of cities, where people have built their own homes on land they do not own.

These settlements go by many names: slums, shantytowns, favelas (in Brazil), townships (in South Africa), or informal settlements. They often lack basic infrastructure like clean water, electricity, sewage systems, and paved roads — because, since the residents have no legal claim to the land, the government and utility companies typically do not provide services to them.

Some of the world's most famous examples include the favelas of Rio de Janeiro (Brazil), Dharavi in Mumbai (India), and Kibera in Nairobi (Kenya). Hundreds of millions of people worldwide live as squatters in such settlements.
How a Squatter Differs from Similar People

It helps to understand this word by comparing it to related terms:

  • A tenant pays rent and has a legal agreement (a lease) with the owner. A squatter pays nothing and has no agreement at all.
  • A trespasser enters a property without permission, but usually just passes through or enters briefly. A squatter actually lives in a place and treats it as their home — they stay.
  • A homeless person does not necessarily occupy a specific building or land. A squatter has specifically settled in and occupies a particular space.

The legal status of squatting varies significantly from place to place.

  • In many countries and states, squatting is a criminal offense — meaning the squatter can be arrested.
  • In other places, it is treated as a civil matter, meaning the property owner cannot have the squatter arrested but must go through a court to legally remove them (a process called eviction). This can sometimes take months or even years.
  • In some places, the law distinguishes between squatting in a residential property (one meant for people to live in) versus squatting in a commercial property (like an office or warehouse), treating these differently.

A squatter is someone who occupies property — a building, a piece of land, or any space — without owning it, paying for it, or having legal permission to be there. In modern usage, this word most often refers to a homeless or impoverished person seeking shelter, or to communities of people building homes on unused land. Historically, it referred to pioneering settlers who occupied government-owned land to farm it. The concept of "squatter's rights" (adverse possession) means that, in some cases and after a very long time, a squatter may even earn legal ownership of the property they have occupied.
15063: A squawk is a sudden, loud, harsh, and unpleasant noise — the kind that feels almost jarring to hear. Think of a parrot screaming, a hen that just got frightened, or a rusty door hinge. The sound is sharp, shrill, and decidedly not musical. It draws attention precisely because it's so grating.

This is the most direct, everyday use of the word.

A squawk is a short, sharp, discordant cry — usually made by a bird, but it can describe similar sounds from other animals or even machines.

What makes it a squawk specifically (and not just a "cry" or a "shriek")? A squawk is:

  • Abrupt — it bursts out suddenly
  • Harsh — not smooth or melodic
  • Loud — it carries
  • Often high-pitched — though not always piercing in a clean, thin way; it has a rough edge

Examples:

  • The parrot let out a squawk when the cat walked past its cage.
  • There was a squawk from the henhouse — something had startled the chickens.
  • The old radio gave a squawk of static before the signal cleared.

Notice that last example — the word extends naturally beyond animals. Any sudden, harsh, unpleasant burst of sound can be called a squawk if it has that rough, jarring quality.

In informal, mostly American English, a squawk also means a loud or vigorous complaint, objection, or grumble — especially one that feels a bit whiny or self-righteous.

The connection to the first meaning is intuitive: just as a frightened hen squawks loudly and persistently, a person who's annoyed or wronged "squawks" — they make noise about it, they protest, they grumble.

This meaning carries a slight dismissive or humorous tone. When you call someone's complaint a "squawk," you're usually suggesting it's a bit overblown, petty, or not entirely warranted — or at least, that it's very vocal.

Examples:

  • There were a few squawks from customers about the new policy, but most people accepted it.
  • The team manager heard not a single squawk from the players about the early morning practice.
  • His loudest squawk was about the parking fees — he went on about it for days.

This is a more specialized meaning, but it's widely used in aviation, military contexts, air traffic control, and anything related to aircraft — so it's worth knowing.

In aviation, a squawk refers to a four-digit numerical code that a pilot dials into an aircraft's transponder (a radio device that identifies the plane to radar systems). Air traffic control assigns each aircraft a specific squawk code, which makes it possible for controllers on the ground to identify individual planes on their radar screens among potentially dozens of others.

For example, an air traffic controller might tell a pilot: "Squawk 4521" — meaning "set your transponder to code 4521 so we can track you."

As a noun, "the squawk" or "their squawk" simply refers to this four-digit code itself.

There are also a few universal emergency squawk codes that every pilot in the world knows:

  • 7700 — General emergency
  • 7600 — Loss of radio communication (can't talk to controllers)
  • 7500 — Hijacking in progress

If a plane is "squawking 7700," it means its squawk code is set to 7700 — a silent signal to air traffic control that something is very wrong.

Examples:

  • The controller asked the pilot to confirm her squawk — the code wasn't showing up on radar.
  • The aircraft was squawking 7700, so emergency services were immediately put on standby.
  • Each plane in the holding pattern had a different squawk to keep them separated on the display.

The word entered aviation slang precisely because of its first meaning — these transponder signals originally produced audible tones, and the idea of a device "crying out" its identity stuck.

MeaningContextTone

All three meanings share a common thread: something calling attention to itself suddenly and loudly, whether it's a bird in alarm, a person with a grievance, or an aircraft announcing its identity.

  • In everyday life, a squawk is the harsh, startling cry of a bird or a similarly jarring sound.
  • In informal conversation, a squawk is a noisy complaint — vocal, blunt, and sometimes petty.
  • In aviation and technical contexts, a squawk is the four-digit transponder code an aircraft broadcasts to radar systems.

The sound isn't gentle. A squawk is never soft or melodious. If you describe a sound as a squawk, you're explicitly saying it was rough and unpleasant. A songbird doesn't squawk — a parrot, a seagull, or a frightened chicken does.

The complaint meaning is informal. You'd use it in casual speech or writing, not in formal reports or serious professional contexts. It has a slightly playful edge.

The aviation meaning is very specific. Outside of aviation, aerospace, or military contexts, most people won't use "squawk" to mean a transponder code. But if you ever read a news story about an aircraft emergency, you'll almost certainly encounter it.

Quantity matters slightly. You can have a squawk (one complaint or one code) or squawks (multiple complaints). "There were squawks from all sides" suggests many people protesting.

That covers the full picture of "squawk" as a noun — from startled hens to disgruntled customers to radar screens.
15064: To squawk is to make — or say something in — a loud, harsh, sharp, and unpleasant cry or sound. Think of the noise a parrot, a seagull, or a frightened chicken makes. That grating, piercing sound that instantly grabs your attention but is not at all pleasant to hear? That is a squawk. The word itself almost sounds like what it describes.

1. Making a Harsh Cry (Animals and People)

When a bird or an animal squawks, it lets out a sudden, loud, rough, shrill sound — usually out of fear, surprise, or protest.

  • The parrot squawked when the cat walked into the room.
  • The seagulls squawked and fought over the piece of bread.

Humans can squawk too. If a person squawks, they make a sudden, undignified, uncontrolled sound — like a yelp or a screech — often from shock or pain.

  • She squawked in surprise when cold water splashed on her back.
  • The toddler squawked when his toy was taken away.

Notice that squawking is never graceful or musical. It is always a little jarring or ugly. That is central to the word.

2. Complaining Loudly and Noisily (Informal)

This is the most common way the word is used for humans in everyday speech. When someone squawks about something, they are complaining, protesting, or grumbling in a loud, persistent, and somewhat irritating way.

  • Customers squawked about the new policy for weeks.
  • He squawked about the long wait until the manager came out.
  • Don't squawk — just fix the problem.

The key feeling here is that the complaint sounds excessive, whiny, or annoying — like the person is making more noise than the situation truly deserves. When you say someone "squawked," you are subtly suggesting their protest was loud but not entirely dignified. It carries a mild tone of dismissiveness toward the complainer.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "She complained about the noise." — Neutral. Just a fact.
  • "She squawked about the noise." — Suggests she went on and on, loudly, in a way that was a bit much.

3. A Technical Aviation Meaning

In the world of aviation, squawk has a very specific and official meaning. When air traffic control tells a pilot to squawk a code, it means the pilot must dial a specific four-digit number into the aircraft's transponder — a device that sends out a signal so the plane can be identified on radar.

  • "Squawk 2400," the controller told the pilot.
  • The aircraft squawked the emergency code 7700.

In this context, squawking is the act of broadcasting an identification signal. The pilot "squawks" a code, meaning they set the transponder to that code and the plane is then visible and identifiable to air traffic control on their screens. This is a technical, not a casual, use.

Across all its uses, "squawk" always carries the idea of something sudden, loud, and a little harsh — whether it is a bird crying out, a person yelping in surprise, someone complaining noisily, or an aircraft sending out a signal. It is never soft, never musical, never graceful.

Squawking implies a degree of annoyance. When you describe an animal's sound as a squawk, you are signaling that the sound is unpleasant. When you describe a person as squawking, you are usually (gently) mocking how they expressed themselves.

Squawking is reactive. Animals squawk when startled or threatened. People squawk when something bothers them. It is almost always a response to something — not a calm, pre-planned act.

The word is informal when used for humans. You would never write in a formal report that "the shareholders squawked about the losses." But in a newspaper column, a casual article, or everyday conversation, it fits perfectly.

Picture a parrot sitting calmly on a perch. Someone walks by and accidentally bumps its cage. The parrot squawks — a loud, jarring cry of alarm. Now picture a customer at a shop who has been overcharged. He squawks — he raises his voice, complains loudly and repeatedly, causing everyone around to feel a little uncomfortable. Both images share the same energy: sudden, loud, unpleasant, and impossible to ignore.

That is exactly what squawk means.
15065: To squeak means to produce a short, sharp, high-pitched sound — one that is thin and piercing in quality, but not very loud and not long-lasting. Think of the sound a mouse makes, or the sound of a door with a rusty hinge. That brief, sharp, high little sound — that is a squeak.

To understand the word deeply, it helps to understand what kind of sound qualifies as a squeak. A squeak has three defining qualities:

  • High-pitched: It is not a deep or low sound. It sits at the upper end of the sound range.
  • Short: It does not drag on. It appears and disappears quickly.
  • Thin and sharp: It is not a full, rich sound. It has a narrow, almost needle-like quality to it.

If a sound is too long, it becomes a squeal (like a pig, or a car's brakes). If it is too low and drawn-out, it becomes a creak (like an old wooden floorboard settling slowly). If it is very loud and harsh, it becomes a screech. A squeak sits between these — small, quick, and high.

Animals

Small animals squeak naturally. Mice squeak. Rats squeak. Hamsters, gerbils, and other small rodents squeak. Young animals of many species — puppies, kittens, chicks — often squeak before they develop their mature voices.

The mouse squeaked and ran behind the cupboard.
The baby bird squeaked every time its mother flew away.

Objects

Many everyday objects squeak when they are under friction, stress, or pressure, especially when they are old, dry, or poorly maintained.

  • A door hinge without oil squeaks when you open or close the door.
  • A floorboard squeaks when you step on it.
  • New leather shoes or rubber-soled shoes often squeak on hard floors.
  • A rubber toy (like a rubber duck) squeaks when you press it.
  • A wheel or axle that needs grease will squeak as it turns.
  • A bed spring can squeak when someone sits or shifts their weight.
  • A swing at a playground squeaks as it moves back and forth.

The old door squeaked loudly as he pushed it open.
Her new shoes squeaked on the polished marble floor.
The wheels of the cart squeaked as she pushed it down the corridor.

People (voice)

A person's voice can squeak — usually when they are frightened, surprised, or when they speak in an unusually high and strained voice. It is also common during adolescence when a boy's voice is "breaking" and jumping between registers.

She squeaked in surprise when the door slammed behind her.
His voice squeaked with nervousness during the presentation.
"Help!" he squeaked, barely loud enough for anyone to hear.

Notice in that last example: "barely loud enough." This is important — squeaking implies smallness and weakness of sound. A squeak is not a powerful sound. It hints at smallness, vulnerability, or lack of force.

Beyond the literal sound, "squeak" has developed figurative meanings that are used very frequently in everyday English.

1. To "squeak by" or "squeak through" — to barely manage

This is perhaps the most common figurative use. When you squeak by or squeak through something, you barely succeed, barely pass, or barely survive — with almost no margin to spare. The image is of something passing through a very tight, narrow gap, making a small desperate sound as it just barely fits.

She squeaked through the final exam with exactly the minimum passing marks.
The team squeaked by their opponents with a single point to spare.
He squeaked through the job interview — it was not a confident performance, but he got the role.
The business squeaked through the financial crisis without going bankrupt.

The key idea here: it was close. It almost didn't happen. There was no comfort zone.

2. To "squeak out" — to barely produce or achieve something

Similar to "squeak through," but used more when talking about barely producing a result.

The candidate squeaked out a victory in the election by fewer than 200 votes.
They squeaked out a win in the final ten seconds of the match.

3. To squeak (informal) — to inform on someone, to tell on someone

In informal, colloquial use (especially British English), "to squeak" can mean to inform on someone — that is, to secretly tell an authority (police, a teacher, a boss) about someone else's wrongdoing. This use is less common than the others, but worth knowing. It comes from the same family as "squeal" (a more common word for the same idea).

He was afraid one of them would squeak to the police.

Since you want a complete picture, here are the closely related words born from "squeak":

Squeak (noun) — the sound itself.

I heard a squeak coming from inside the wall.
The door gave a loud squeak.

Squeaky (adjective) — something that squeaks, or that has the quality of a squeak; describes a high, thin, sharp-sounding voice or object.

The gate had a squeaky hinge.
She spoke in a squeaky voice.
"Squeaky clean" is a very common phrase meaning completely clean, or, figuratively, having a completely spotless reputation — no scandals, no faults, no secrets.
The politician tried to maintain a squeaky-clean image.

Squeaker (noun) — something or someone that squeaks. Also used informally to describe a very close contest or competition — one decided by the tiniest of margins.

The election was a real squeaker — decided by only a handful of votes.

"Not a squeak" — complete silence; no noise or response at all.

We waited for news, but not a squeak from them for three days.
I called his name twice. Not a squeak.

"Squeaky clean" — spotlessly clean (literal) or having an irreproachable, faultless reputation (figurative).

After the scandal, the company worked hard to appear squeaky clean.

"Squeak by/through" — barely manage to pass or survive something (covered above in detail).
How It Feels to Use This Word

One of the most useful things to understand about "squeak" is the emotional and sensory texture of the word. It is a word that carries a feeling of smallness, tightness, and barely-enough-ness. Whether it is the literal sound (small, thin, barely audible) or the figurative meanings (barely making it through), the word always suggests something operating at its absolute minimum — just enough, and no more.

When a door squeaks, it is telling you it needs attention — it is at the edge of functioning smoothly. When a person squeaks through an exam, they are at the edge of passing. This is the soul of the word: the very edge, the tight margin, the small and strained.

UseMeaning

In short: squeak as a verb means to make a short, sharp, high-pitched sound (used literally for animals, objects, and voices), and figuratively, to barely manage or survive something (squeak by, squeak through, squeak out). It always carries a sense of smallness and tightness — just enough, and no more.
15066: "Squeal" has two very different lives as a verb — one literal and one figurative. In its literal sense, it describes a particular kind of sound. In its figurative (slang) sense, it describes a particular kind of betrayal. Both meanings are widely used, so you need to know both.
Meaning 1: To Make a High-Pitched, Sharp, Drawn-Out Sound

This is the core, original meaning of the word.

When something or someone squeals, they produce a sound that has three qualities at once:

  • High-pitched — not deep or low, but sharp and piercing
  • Loud — noticeable, not soft or quiet
  • Drawn-out — it doesn't end in a split second; it stretches for a moment

Think of it as the sound of something under pressure — whether emotional pressure or physical friction.

Who or what can squeal?

Animals:
The most classic image is a pig — pigs squeal. It is their signature distress sound. A rabbit caught by a predator squeals. A mouse squeals when frightened. If you know what a pig sounds like when scared or hurt, you already have the perfect mental image of a squeal.

People:
Humans squeal too, usually when caught in a sudden surge of strong emotion.

  • A child who sees a pile of birthday presents might squeal with excitement.
  • Someone who is suddenly grabbed from behind might squeal in fright.
  • A person who is tickled might squeal with laughter.
  • Someone who touches something painfully hot might squeal in pain.

Notice that people usually squeal involuntarily — it bursts out of them before they can control it. It is raw, unfiltered emotion escaping through sound.

Objects and machines:
Non-living things can also squeal when friction or mechanical stress creates that same sharp, high-pitched sound.

  • Car brakes squeal when you stop suddenly or when the brake pads are worn out.
  • Tires squeal when a car turns a corner too fast.
  • A door hinge that needs oil can squeal every time the door opens.
  • A microphone held too close to a speaker squeals — that sharp, painful feedback sound.

The emotion inside the word

When used for people or animals, a squeal almost always signals intensity. The person or animal is not mildly happy or slightly uncomfortable — they are really excited, really scared, or really in pain. The sound is an overflow of feeling.

This is why "squeal" sounds more vivid and alive than simply saying "cry out" or "make a noise." It tells you the pitch, the volume, and the emotional intensity all at once.

Examples in sentences

  • The little girl squealed with delight when she saw the puppy.
  • He squealed in pain when the nurse gave him the injection.
  • The car's tires squealed as it sped around the corner.
  • The piglets squealed when the farmer tried to catch them.
  • The microphone squealed, and everyone in the hall winced.

This meaning is completely different and is used in informal, conversational language.

To squeal on someone means to secretly go to the police, a teacher, a boss, or any authority figure and tell them about something wrong that person did. In short — to betray someone by reporting them.

This is essentially the same as "to snitch," "to rat on someone," "to tell on someone," or "to grass" (British English).

Why this word specifically?

The connection to the sound-meaning is intentional and poetic. Informers were thought of like frightened pigs — cowardly, making noise to save their own skin at someone else's expense. The word stuck.

The tone is always negative

"Squeal" in this sense is never neutral. It always carries the idea of disloyalty and cowardice. If you say someone "squealed," you are judging them harshly. You are saying they broke a code of silence or violated the trust of the group to protect themselves.

Compare:

  • "He told the police" — neutral, factual
  • "He squealed to the police" — loaded with contempt; he is a traitor

The person who squeals is sometimes called a squealer — and this is a deeply unflattering label.

Key grammar note

In this meaning, "squeal" almost always appears with "on":

  • squeal on someone

You squeal on the people you are betraying, to the authority you are reporting to.

Examples in sentences

  • Nobody in the gang would squeal on the others, even after they were arrested.
  • He squealed on his partner to get a lighter sentence.
  • Don't squeal on me — I was just trying to help you.
  • The other kids called her a squealer because she told the teacher about the fight.
Meaning 3: To Protest or Complain Loudly (Less Common)

There is a third, less common use of the word. Sometimes people use "squeal" to mean to complain very loudly and dramatically, usually about something that feels unfair.

This is a figurative extension of the sound meaning — imagine someone making a lot of noise in protest, like an animal in distress.

  • Companies squealed when the new regulations were announced.
  • He squealed about the unfairness of it all, but nobody listened.

This usage is fairly informal and is not as common as the first two meanings, but you will encounter it in newspapers and casual speech, often when writers want to convey that the complaining was excessive or undignified.

PhraseMeaning

"Squeal with delight / excitement / laughter" — To make a joyful, high-pitched sound out of happiness.

"Squeal in pain / fear / horror" — To cry out sharply because of a sudden, intense feeling.

"Squeal on someone" — To betray and report someone to authority.

"Squeal to the police / the boss / the teacher" — To go and inform someone in power about another person's wrongdoing.

"Squeal like a pig" — A vivid phrase meaning to cry out loudly in pain or distress, or (in the informer sense) to confess everything without resistance.
Connotations: What the Word Feels Like

• In the sound meaning — the word feels energetic, vivid, and sensory. When you read it, you almost hear it.
  • In the betrayal meaning — the word feels dark, contemptuous, and judgmental. It is not a word you use for someone you respect.
  • In the complaining meaning — the word has a slightly dismissive tone. Calling someone's complaint a "squeal" suggests their protest is dramatic and not entirely dignified.

At its simplest:

Squeal (literal) = to make a sharp, high-pitched, stretched-out cry — out of excitement, fear, pain, or physical friction.

Squeal (slang) = to betray someone by secretly informing on them to an authority — a cowardly act of disloyalty.

Squeal (informal/figurative) = to complain loudly and dramatically.

The sound meaning is universal and used in all contexts — formal writing, fiction, everyday speech. The betrayal meaning is strictly informal and carries a strong negative judgment. If you can picture a frightened pig and a cowardly informer, you will never forget this word.
15067:
If someone is squeamish, they are easily made to feel sick, disgusted, uncomfortable, or faint when they encounter something unpleasant — especially something involving blood, injury, gore, bodily functions, or anything visually or physically disturbing.

The key idea is that their reaction is stronger than what most people would feel. It is an almost involuntary feeling of revulsion or weakness — the person often knows they are not in any real danger, but their body and mind react strongly anyway.

Think of it this way: if someone shows you a small cut on their finger and you feel perfectly fine, but your friend next to you goes pale, feels dizzy, and has to look away — your friend is squeamish.

A squeamish person can be triggered by a wide range of things, most commonly:

  • Blood and wounds — seeing injuries, cuts, surgery, or medical procedures
  • Gore and violence — in real life or even in movies
  • Needles and injections — many people are specifically squeamish about this
  • Bodily functions and fluids — things society generally considers gross
  • Insects or creatures — especially slimy, crawling, or creepy-looking ones
  • Dead things — animals, corpses, or anything decaying
  • Unpleasant smells — though this is less common usage

The word is most naturally used for things that are visually disturbing or physically gross.

The reaction of a squeamish person is both physical and psychological:

Physically, they might feel:

  • Nauseous (like they want to vomit)
  • Dizzy or light-headed
  • Faint or weak in the knees
  • An urgent need to look away

Psychologically, they feel:

  • Deep discomfort or disgust
  • An inability to think about or engage with the thing calmly
  • A strong urge to avoid or escape the situation

Importantly, this is not just a choice to act dramatic. The reaction feels very real and involuntary to the person experiencing it.

Besides physical disgust, squeamish also has a second meaning: being easily disturbed or made uncomfortable by things that seem morally questionable, offensive, or ethically complicated.

In this sense, a squeamish person is overly sensitive or hesitant when it comes to difficult moral territory. They avoid or feel uneasy about things that are ethically grey, controversial, or that require tough decisions.

For example:

  • A journalist who refuses to report on dark or disturbing crimes because they find it too unsettling could be called squeamish.
  • A politician who avoids taking any firm stance on a difficult issue because they don't want to deal with moral conflict might be described as squeamish.

Here, squeamish implies a kind of moral timidity — an unwillingness to face something uncomfortable, even when it needs to be faced.

Squeamish carries a mildly negative connotation. When you call someone squeamish, you are not being harshly critical, but you are suggesting that their reaction is somewhat excessive, overly sensitive, or even a little weak. It implies they need to toughen up or that they are not well-suited for situations that require a strong stomach.

For example, a doctor cannot afford to be squeamish. A soldier, a butcher, a crime scene investigator — these are professions where squeamishness would be a real problem.

However, the word is not a serious insult. It is often used lightly, even affectionately, to tease someone about their sensitivity. If a friend covers their eyes during a horror movie, you might laugh and say, "Oh, don't be so squeamish!"

A person can be squeamish to varying degrees:

  • Mildly squeamish — They feel a little uncomfortable around blood but can manage it.
  • Very squeamish — They cannot watch even a small injection on TV without feeling faint.
  • Squeamish about a specific thing — Someone might be completely fine with gore in movies but specifically squeamish about needles, or fine with everything except insects.

This is why you will often hear phrases like:

  • "a little squeamish"
  • "particularly squeamish about..."
  • "not the least bit squeamish"

Here are examples that show the word in its natural habitat:

  1. She was too squeamish to watch the surgery scene in the film, so she closed her eyes.
  2. He has always been squeamish about blood — even a small cut makes him feel dizzy.
  3. You can't be squeamish if you want to work in a hospital.
  4. The documentary was not for squeamish viewers — it showed real battlefield injuries.
  5. He's squeamish about conflict and always avoids difficult conversations at work. (moral sense)
  6. Don't be so squeamish — it's just a spider!
  7. She wasn't the least bit squeamish; she calmly dressed the wound without flinching.

To sharpen your understanding, here is what squeamish does not mean:

  • It does not mean scared of danger. Fear is about being afraid something will harm you. A squeamish person is disgusted or sickened, even when they know they are perfectly safe. You can be squeamish about a dead insect — it can't hurt you, but it still makes you feel sick.
  • It does not mean weak in general. A very brave, physically strong person can still be squeamish about needles.
  • It does not mean shy or introverted. Those words are about social behavior. Squeamish is specifically about reactions to unpleasant or disturbing stimuli.

Squeamish means being easily made to feel sick, faint, or deeply uncomfortable by unpleasant things — especially blood, gore, or anything physically gross. It can also mean being overly sensitive about moral or ethical discomfort. The word implies that the reaction is stronger than usual and suggests a certain lack of toughness or tolerance for the unpleasant.
15068: "Squeeze" means to press something firmly from two or more sides at the same time, usually with your fingers, hands, or body. Think of holding an orange in your palm and pressing it tightly — that is squeezing. The pressure applied from multiple directions is the central image of this word. Every other meaning you'll learn below grows naturally from it.

Pressing to force something out

The most direct use is pressing something to make a substance come out of it. The pressure is the cause; something emerging is the result.

She squeezed the lemon over the salad. He squeezed the toothpaste out of the tube. Squeeze a little glue onto the paper.

This also works more broadly — you can "squeeze the last bit of effort" out of yourself, meaning you extracted absolutely everything you had.

Pressing as a physical gesture of emotion

When you squeeze a person or part of their body, it is usually warm and affectionate — a way of communicating something through touch. It is firm but not painful.

She squeezed his hand to comfort him. He squeezed her in a tight hug. The child squeezed her toy against her chest.

The physical action is identical (pressing firmly), but here the purpose is to express love, support, or reassurance.

Pressing a trigger

In the context of firearms, the correct and precise word is "squeeze" — not "pull."

He squeezed the trigger carefully.

Fitting into a tight physical space

If a space is very narrow but you manage to get through or into it, you squeeze. The idea is that your body is being pressed on both sides as you pass through, like forcing something through a narrow gap.

She squeezed through the small gap in the fence. They squeezed five people into a tiny car. He squeezed past the other passengers. Can you squeeze one more book onto that shelf?

This is extremely common in everyday English. Any time a space is barely enough, "squeeze" is the natural word.

Fitting into a tight schedule

The exact same logic — barely fitting into a tight space — applies to time. When your day is almost full but you manage to fit something in, you squeeze it in.

The doctor can squeeze you in at 4 PM. I squeezed a quick workout into my morning. Can we squeeze this call in before the meeting?

Pressuring someone to extract something from them

When you "squeeze" a person in this sense, you apply pressure on them — through demands, threats, or persistent force — to get money, information, a confession, or something else of value. This use carries a forceful or slightly aggressive tone.

The landlord squeezed the tenants for higher rent. The detective squeezed the suspect for a confession. Small businesses were being squeezed by rising costs and falling income.

The image is still the same: pressure applied to force something out. It is just that here, what comes out is not juice — it is money, information, or compliance.

Barely achieving something

When a result is reached with great difficulty, or by the smallest possible margin, you "squeeze" it out — as though forcing it through an impossibly tight gap.

The team squeezed out a narrow victory in the final minute. She squeezed through the exam with just a passing grade.

Squeeze in — to fit something or someone into a tight space or schedule.
Can you squeeze in one more appointment?

Squeeze out — to extract something by pressure; or to gradually force someone out of a position or market.
The big supermarkets squeezed out the smaller local shops.

Squeeze through — to pass through a physically tight space, or to barely get through a difficult situation.
We squeezed through the narrow alley. She squeezed through the round of interviews.

Squeeze past — to move past someone when there is very little room.
Excuse me, can I squeeze past?

Put the squeeze on someone — to pressure someone strongly to make them do what you want.
The bank put the squeeze on the company to repay its debt.

Squeeze blood from a stone — to try to get something from a source that has absolutely nothing to give; used when something feels completely impossible.
Getting him to admit he was wrong is like squeezing blood from a stone.

Every single use of this word shares one underlying image: applying pressure to force something through a tight space — whether that space is physical (a gap in a fence), time-based (a packed schedule), relational (extracting something from an unwilling person), or metaphorical (barely winning something against the odds).

If you hold onto the image of pressing an orange firmly in your hand — squeezing it from all sides until the juice has nowhere to go but out — you have the soul of this word. Every other meaning is just that same force applied to a different kind of "space" or a different kind of "something to extract." The rest follows naturally.
15069:
To squelch something means to press down on it with enough force to crush or silence it completely — stopping it dead in its tracks, leaving no room for it to survive or continue. Think of it as the verbal version of placing your foot firmly on something and pushing it flat.

The word lives in two worlds: the physical and the figurative. Both are important, but the figurative use is by far the more common one in everyday life.

In the physical world, squelch describes what happens when something soft, wet, or mushy is pressed or stepped on, and in doing so, produces a wet, sucking sound — that horrible, satisfying noise mud makes when you walk through it.

"Her boots squelched through the muddy field with every step."
"He squelched the soaking wet cloth in his hands."

Notice that squelching isn't just any crushing. It specifically involves softness and wetness. The thing being squelched doesn't crack or shatter — it gives way, oozing and making that signature sound. A soggy shoe squelches. A dry brick does not.

This is where squelch is most powerful and most commonly used. Here, it means to completely and decisively shut something down — an idea, a feeling, a rumor, a person, or a situation — with authority and finality. There's no gradual fading here. When something is squelched, it is stopped cold.

1. Squelching ideas, proposals, or plans
When someone in a position of power kills an idea before it can go anywhere, they squelch it.

"The principal squelched the students' plan to hold a protest on school grounds."
"Every suggestion she made in the meeting was squelched before she could even finish explaining it."

2. Squelching rumors
To squelch a rumor means to stop it from spreading by addressing it directly and firmly.

"The company released a statement to squelch rumors that it was going bankrupt."

3. Squelching feelings or impulses from within yourself
You can also squelch something inside you — a feeling, an urge, a reaction — by pushing it down before it surfaces.

"She squelched the urge to cry and kept her face completely still."
"He squelched his frustration and answered the question politely."

This internal use is particularly expressive. It captures that effort of consciously suppressing something that is trying to rise up inside you.

4. Squelching a rebellion, uprising, or resistance
When authority puts down organized opposition — quickly and with force — that's squelching.

"The army squelched the revolt within 48 hours."

5. Squelching a person
You can squelch a person by silencing them sharply — putting them firmly in their place with a word, a look, or a response that leaves no room for comeback.

"The professor squelched the student's arrogant remark with a single, devastating reply."
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

Squelch is not a soft or neutral word. It carries force, decisiveness, and finality. When something is squelched, it doesn't survive — not even a little. The word also often carries a slight edge of authority or even harshness. The person doing the squelching has power, and they use it without hesitation.

This is how it differs from similar words:

  • Suppress is cooler and more formal — it simply means to hold something back. Squelch is more vivid and forceful.
  • Silence means to stop sound or speech. Squelch goes further — it implies the thing is not just silenced but thoroughly put down.
  • Stifle means to hold back or prevent something (often gently, like stifling a laugh). Squelch is harder and more complete.
  • Dampen means to reduce enthusiasm or energy slightly. Squelch doesn't reduce — it eliminates.

The physical origin of the word (crushing something wet and soft underfoot) bleeds into the figurative meaning beautifully. When you squelch an idea or a rumor, you are — in your imagination — stepping on it and pressing it flat.

In real usage, squelch almost always appears with an object — something is being squelched. You'll often see it paired with words like: rumors, fears, hopes, ideas, rebellion, opposition, criticism, doubts, feelings, plans.

"Officials worked to squelch fears about the new policy."
"She could not squelch her growing sense of dread."
"The teacher squelched the side conversation with a single glance."

• It does not mean to gradually reduce something (that's "diminish" or "dampen").
  • It does not mean to simply disagree with something. You can disagree and still let something continue. Squelching ends it entirely.
  • In its figurative sense, it has nothing to do with wetness or sound — those are purely physical associations.

To squelch something is to crush it completely and decisively — whether physically (by pressing something wet and soft) or figuratively (by shutting down an idea, feeling, rumor, or person with finality and force).
